Listen to this article Share You celebrate the sale. The payment clears, the confirmation email goes out, and you turn your attention elsewhere. Meanwhile, the person who trusted you with money waits for a sign that you care. No message comes. No thanks. No hint that you remember their name. In its Future of Customer Experience study, PwC surveyed 4,000 people in the United States and 11,000 in 11 other countries. Of those surveyed, 74% wanted more human interaction from companies, not less. You have felt this yourself. You bought a coat or a meal kit, enjoyed the moment, and never heard from the seller again. Months later, you could not name the shop. Silence has a price, and the figures show it. Frederick Reichheld of Bain & Company found that a 5% rise in customer retention can lift profits by between 25% and 95%. The same PwC study found that 32% of customers would leave a brand they love after a single bad experience, and 60% would leave because of unfriendly service. I believe this silence, not price or product, explains why customers rarely buy from you twice. Three habits send buyers away, and each one can change. You treat the sale as the Finish A sale marks a beginning. The buyer hands over money because hope sits behind the purchase: hope that the parcel arrives, that the product works, and that someone answers if it fails. When you stop at the till, you walk away from that hope. Think of a host who invites guests, takes their coats, and leaves the room. Nobody returns for a second party. Customers come back to businesses that answer those questions before anyone asks them. Send a message after the sale. Thank the buyer by name, ask how the product performs, and share a tip on its use. Silence feels like indifference, and indifference hurts, even when nobody intends it. A note costs minutes. Its absence costs years of custom, and buyers rarely complain about it. They drift to a rival who notices them, and you never learn why. You let problems grow A buyer who has a problem and cannot reach you feels abandoned. Most never say a word. They leave, they tell friends, and they write a review that you read months later with regret. Each hour of delay tells the buyer that you rank them below your own comfort. Open a route for complaints. Reply within hours, not days. A fast reply says that the buyer matters. Apologise without excuses, then fix the fault. Pride gets in the way, yet customers judge you by your response to a fault, not by the fault itself. A buyer whose problem you solve with care often trusts you more than a buyer who never met a problem at all. You forget that people want to feel seen Behind each transaction stands a person with bills, worries and hopes. That person wants to know that the money they spent mattered to someone. Buyers can find your product elsewhere, often at a price that matches yours, so price does not bind them to you. Memory does. A business that recalls a name, an order and a preference earns a place in someone’s life. A business that treats buyers as rows on a spreadsheet earns refund requests. Templates, scripts and stock phrases tell buyers that nobody listens, so write to people in words you would use across a table. Discounts attract bargain hunters. Care attracts people who stay. I have watched owners pour money into advertising while the people who already trust them drift away. It breaks my heart, because the remedy costs nothing but attention. Open your inbox today. Do not wait for a campaign or a budget. Write to the buyers who purchased this week. Thank them, ask what went well, and ask what failed. Then act on what they say, and tell them you did. The cost is an hour, and the return is a customer who comes back. Customers do not leave because they dislike you. They leave because they feel forgotten. Remember them, and they will remember you.
